1:
The opening verse turns on a single vowel, and the two who face it disagree about what to do. Ellicott reports that a decided preponderance of manuscript authority compels the reading let us have, though the older reading would seem to make the best sense, and objects that a hortatory element is thereby introduced which does not naturally belong to the passage; he suggests a very early copyist's error afterwards corrected by conjecture, noting that in the two oldest manuscripts the familiar reading appears as a correction. Robertson allows no such hesitation: the subjunctive is the correct text beyond a doubt, and it is curious how perverse many real scholars have been on this word and phrase, one calling it difficult if not impossible to explain. His own explanation turns on tense, since the mode is volitive and the present expresses linear action, so that the exhortation is not make peace, which the ingressive aorist would have meant, but keep on enjoying the peace already possessed. Barnes and Calvin both read the chapter as showing the effects of a doctrine already established, Calvin calling the whole of it amplification calculated to explain as much as to confirm.

Calvin defines the peace narrowly and then tests it against experience. It means tranquillity of conscience arising from feeling oneself reconciled to God; and whoever seeks that tranquillity by works labours in vain, since either his heart is asleep through disregard of God's judgment or else it is full of trembling and dread until it reposes on Christ, who alone is our peace. On the access, Clarke insists the privilege is continuing rather than momentary: we are not brought to God for the purpose of an interview but to remain with him, to be his household and by faith to behold his face. Barnes and Robertson both note the rarity of the word, which occurs elsewhere only twice, and Robertson adds that grace is here a field into which we have been introduced and where we stand. Ellicott points out that the word rendered rejoice is the one used elsewhere for boasting, so that the Christian has his boasting though it is not based on his own merits. The note printed with Calvin observes that the style here is the prophets' rather than the ordinary Greek, the first two verses forming a pair of distichs in which the second restates the first and adds one clause, so that justified by faith answers to this grace wherein we stand.

Calvin meets an objection before drawing out the chain: lest anyone scoff that Christians with all their glorying are strangely harassed in this life, he answers that the calamities do not merely fail to prevent blessedness but promote the glorying, and adds that the saints are not free from dread or undistressed by bitterness, since there is no patience where there is no feeling of bitterness. Clarke explains the word for patience as endurance under trial without loss or deterioration, a metaphor taken from the refining of metals, and adds that they do not speak from sudden raptures. Ellicott collects the parallel exhortations to glory in persecution and quotes Bacon's aphorism that prosperity is the blessing of the Old Testament and adversity of the New. Wesley reports the context of the objection, that the Jews urged the persecuted state of Christians as inconsistent with being the Messiah's people, and quotes Theodoret that the apostle says not that we patiently endure afflictions but that we rejoice in them. On the closing clause, Barnes traces the phrase about not being ashamed to the psalm about fathers who trusted and were not confounded; and the note with Calvin distinguishes two hopes in the passage, one hanging on God's testimony and the later one gathered from what the believer finds within.
6:
Henry frames the section as a descent to the spring-head. The streams of privilege are very sweet, he says, but run them up and the source is found in Christ's dying for us, so that everything comes flowing through that precious blood; and he divides what follows into three, the persons died for, the fruits of the death, and the parallel between the two Adams. On the character those persons were under, Henry works the two descriptions separately: without strength means a condition not merely sad but one they were unable to help themselves out of, lost with no visible way open for recovery, which is why the help is said to come in due time, God's manner being to help at a dead lift so that his own power may be the more magnified; and ungodly means not merely helpless and therefore likely to perish but guilty and therefore deserving to perish, not merely worthless but obnoxious to the holy God. Barnes states the design of the comparison that follows, that it illustrates the love of God by setting it beside the highest human benevolence, since none would be willing to die for a man seeking to injure them, whereas Christ was willing to die for bitter foes.

Whether righteous and good differ is the section's real question, and the two grammarians take opposite sides. Robertson quotes Lightfoot for all the difference in the world between them, shown from Plato and from Christian writers, and defines it as a difference of sympathy, the righteous man being absolutely without it while the good man is beneficent and kind; on that reading it takes courage even in the case of the kindly man to make the supreme sacrifice. Ellicott grants a slight distinction of the same sort, that to be righteous is to direct the will in obedience to an external standard while to be good is to have a natural goodness or benevolence of disposition, but then says the distinction is not insisted on here and the two words are used almost convertibly; he also canvasses and rejects two other readings, that the phrase might be neuter and mean in a good cause, and that the word might bear the special sense of benefactor. Clarke supplies the rabbinic scheme of four classes distinguished by what men say about mine and thine, the just being those who render each his own, the pious those who give up all for a neighbour, and the impious those who take all and give nothing, then asks who would die for one of the first class.

Calvin's rendering omits the clause about the good man altogether, and the note printed with him marks the omission and supplies the material: the just is he who acts as justice requires, on the rabbinic formula about mine and thine, while the good is the kind and beneficent man whom Cicero described as one who does good to those he can. Calvin himself takes the connecting particle as affirmative rather than causal and paraphrases the whole: such an example is most rare among men, that one dies for a just man, though it may sometimes happen; but grant that, and still for an ungodly man none will be found willing to die, and this is what Christ has done. On the verb rendered commendeth, Ellicott notes that the English happily covers a double sense, since the Greek is used both of things in the sense of prove or establish and of persons in the sense of recommend, while Calvin argues that confirming suits best here because the object was not to excite gratitude but to strengthen the confidence of our souls. Robertson observes that the ground of the love was not that we were Jews or Greeks, rich or poor, righteous or good, but plain sinners; Clarke says God set the act in the most conspicuous light.
9:
The argument here is one from the greater to the less, and each of them states it in his own terms. Robertson puts it shortest: the great thing is the justification in Christ's blood, so the final salvation is less of a mystery. Barnes expands the reasoning, that it is much more reasonable to expect the lesser thing because there are fewer obstacles in the way, since if God overcame everything standing between him and enemies, we have far more reason to expect protection now that we are friends; and he adds that being purchased by that blood bestows on us a value proportionate to the price of the redemption and is itself a pledge that what was so dearly bought will be kept. Gill presses the connection as a certainty rather than a probability, that justification and salvation are inseparably joined so that whoever is justified shall be saved, and explains the emphasis on his blood as marking a violent death and not the blood of bulls and goats. Calvin reads the following verse as an explanation of this one amplified by a comparison between life and death, and glosses by his life as meaning through him being alive at God's right hand with every power committed to him.

Wesley stops the exposition to answer a theological objection nobody else raises. Is there then wrath in God, he asks; is not wrath a human passion, and how can a human passion be in God? He answers first by a counter-question, whether love is not equally a human passion, and then directly: wrath in man and love in man are human passions, but wrath in God is not a human passion, nor is love as it is in God, so that the inspired writers ascribe both to God only in an analogical sense. Calvin raises a difficulty of his own about the sequence, that the apostle seems inconsistent with himself, since if the death of Christ was a pledge of the divine love toward us it is hard to see how we were at the same time enemies. Ellicott measures the two intervals in the argument and finds them unequal: the distance separating enmity from reconciliation is large and that separating reconciliation from salvation small, though a difference remains, reconciliation being the initial act and the removal of guilt while salvation is the end of the Christian career, the one specially due to the death and the other brought about rather by the continued agency of the risen Saviour.

Clarke objects to a word in the received version and argues the point at length. It was certainly improper, he says, to translate the noun at the close as atonement rather than reconciliation, since the cognate verb means to reconcile and is so rendered by the translators everywhere else it occurs; the word does not here mean the atonement as generally understood, that is the sacrificial death, but rather the effect of it, the removal of the enmity and the consequent change of our state, the preposition and verb together yielding a thorough change from enmity to friendship. Barnes marks the progression in the joy: earlier the rejoicing was in tribulation and in hope of glory, but here it is in God himself, in his existence and attributes, and this is a characteristic of true piety, since the sinner finds no pleasure in him and deems him unqualified for universal empire. Ellicott notes that a word must be supplied from the previous verse and that the state described is active rather than passive, reconciliation in the present being a foretaste of glory to come. Clarke adds that the enmity in every human heart usually goes unsuspected, one property of sin being to blind the understanding so that men do not know their own state.
12:
Everyone notices that the sentence breaks off before its second half arrives. Ellicott says the clause about sin and death entering by one man ought to have been answered by one about grace and life entering by one man, but a difficulty occurs at the very outset and the rapidity with which ideas throng into the writer's brain breaks the even flow of the sentence. Robertson describes the same interruption, that the comparison between Adam's sin and the redemptive work is begun and the second member never given, the writer turning instead to problems about sin and death and starting over again three verses later. Calvin explains why the comparison was needed: since Christ came to redeem us from the calamity into which Adam precipitated his posterity, we cannot see clearly what we have in Christ except by having what we lost in Adam set before us; but he warns that all things on both sides are not similar, which is why an exception follows. Chrysostom accounts for the whole turn medically, that as the best physicians take pains to discover the source of diseases and go to the very fountain of the mischief, so the writer, having shown justification from several quarters, now confirms it from its opposites, death and sin.

The problem of the interval is stated most sharply by Ellicott. Sin was in the world from Adam downwards as a matter of history, but why guilt, and why death, the punishment of guilt? The man before Moses sinned, yet could not rightly be condemned until there was a law telling him plainly the difference between right and wrong. Ellicott observes that the law of nature is left out of consideration here, since the apostle applies that argument to his contemporaries and does not throw its operation back into the primitive ages. Robertson answers differently, that sin was there before Moses because the Jews were like Gentiles who had the law of reason and conscience, and that what the law added was responsibility and guilt; he glosses the verb for imputing as a commercial term found in inscriptions and papyri for entering an item to someone's account. Wesley quotes Theodoret for a reading nobody else offers, that until the law means not until the beginning of the law but until its end, so that while the law reigned sin had power. Clarke draws the conclusion the passage is usually taken to support, that men are not subjected to death for their own transgressions but for Adam's.

Barnes personifies the reign and lists what makes it terrible: it is absolute, striking whom it pleases and when; there is no escape, since all must bow to its sceptre; it is universal over old and young alike; and it would be an eternal reign were it not for the gospel. Clarke sets out the argument as four propositions taken from Taylor: sin was in the world during the interval, law was not, the sins were therefore not imputed unto death since men transgressed no rule with death annexed, and yet death reigned. Wesley applies the clause about those who had not sinned after the similitude to infants who never sinned as Adam did in their own persons, and reads the two men as public persons and federal heads, one the fountain of sin and death by his offence and the other of righteousness and life by his free gift. Robertson agrees Adam is a type in holding a relation to those affected by the headship, while cautioning that the parallel is not precise. Ellicott admits the point is introduced in a rhetorically faulty way and excuses it by a circumstance of composition, that the letter was dictated and probably never revised by its author.
15:
Ellicott sets the contrast out as a table of parallels, pairing the persons of the action, the action itself, its character, the persons affected, and its proximate and ulterior effects, so that the differences are thrown into relief by the resemblances. He then presses a translation point with doctrinal weight: throughout the passage the reading should be the one and the many rather than one and many, since the many means mankind generally, and he quotes Lightfoot quoting Bentley that by this accurate version some hurtful mistakes about partial redemption and absolute reprobation would have been avoided. Robertson takes the opposite view of the same words, holding it unnecessary to the argument that the many in each case correspond, since one relates to Adam and the other to Christ. Wesley maps the structure instead, that the fall and the free gift differ in amplitude, that the two men differ in power, that the reason for both is then subjoined, and that the offence and the gift are afterwards compared first as to effect and then as to cause. Calvin warns that the apostle does not state the points of difference minutely but rather forestalls errors, and that none of the repetitions lacks either a corresponding clause or at least an ellipsis.

On the surplus of the gift over the loss Clarke is the most insistent. Quoting the writer he has been following, he argues that the comparison will not hold good in every respect, because the gift bestows blessings far beyond the consequences of the offence which therefore have no relation to it; and this had to be said both to prevent mistakes about the consequences of Adam's offence and about the extent of gospel grace, and because the main design was to prove that grace extends to all men not only so far as it takes off the consequence of the offence, that is death without promise of a resurrection, but also in the surplusage of blessings by which it stretches far beyond that consequence. Barnes marks the successive points of contrast as they come, the first being that the evil flowed from the sin of one man and the benefit from the work of one man, the second that the evil consequences flowed from a single act of guilt while the favours had respect to many acts. Robertson gives the reason for the repeated much more, that as a God of love he delights more in showing mercy than in giving just punishment, so that the gift surpasses the sin.

Calvin draws a polemical conclusion from the difference between one offence and many. Since guilt from a single offence issued in the condemnation of all while the gratuitous gift is efficacious to justify from many offences, it appears that their opinion is impious who taught that we recover nothing by Christ but freedom from original sin; and he adds that the many offences we are freed from include not only those committed before baptism but those by which the saints contract new guilt daily, on account of which they would be justly condemned were they not continually relieved by this grace. Ellicott states the same contrast as a matter of verdicts, the sentence from a single case ending in condemnation while the free gift, prompted by many sins, ends in acquittal. Barnes reads the last verse of the three as condensing the whole subject into a single view, and paraphrases the inference: if under the administration of a just and merciful Being the offence of one gave death so wide a dominion, we have much more reason to expect that those brought under his plan of saving mercy come under a dispensation of life. Clarke personifies death as reigning and known by the destruction of his subjects, and sets against that a reign in life.
18:
The summing-up verse is elliptical, and the commentators fill the gap differently. Barnes says the words for judgment came are not in the Greek but are evidently implied, and reads the whole as a recapitulation resuming the proposition broken off six verses earlier, so that the intervening explanation is designed to convey the real meaning of what is now stated. Ellicott judges those supplied words somewhat too much of a paraphrase and prefers simply the issue was, using the same phrase for the parallel clause. Clarke prints the Greek and renders it word for word, then offers what he thinks anyone without a creed to serve would take from the context: as by one sin all men came into condemnation, so by one righteous act all men came unto justification of life. Calvin calls the sentence defective and completes it by putting two words in the nominative, then distinguishes the noun used from the ordinary word for righteousness, showing from three other places that it means what is adjudged right, so that here it answers to condemnation and means absolution or acquittal as the determination of a judge. Robertson notes only that the first phrase about all men matches the earlier verse and the second matches the qualified statement about those who receive.

Why the law came in at all is the last question, and it turns on a single particle. Robertson lays out the alternatives: it is usual to explain the conjunction as final, expressing God's ultimate purpose, and one modern commentator does so, but Chrysostom explained it as expressing result, which is a proper use of the word, and on that reading the sense is that the trespass did in fact abound, which was the actual effect of the Mosaic law for the Jews and the necessary result of all prohibitions. Wesley states the same conclusion flatly, that the increase of sin was the consequence and not the design of the law's coming in. Barnes reads the verse as an answer to an imagined Jewish objection, that the law of Moses was meant to meet the evils introduced by Adam and so made the apostle's scheme unnecessary; the reply is that its effect was to increase rather than diminish those evils, so that it cannot be pleaded as adapted to overcome them. Clarke takes the verb for entering as coming in privily, on the strength of the only other place it occurs, and applies it to the temporary use of the law; the note printed with Calvin denies that it can be so rendered here.

Ellicott glosses the same verb as a graphic metaphor, that the law came in to the side of the sin already existing and took its place beside it, joining forces with it and so adding to its extent and power; he also corrects the received version's threefold abound, since the original word differs in two of the three places and there has the force of being multiplied or made worse. Clarke supplies the reason the law was needed for that purpose, asking how the finer deviations from a straight line could be ascertained without applying a known straight edge. On the closing sentence Calvin notices that the order of words is deranged and explains why: the simple contrast would have set righteousness against sin, but the apostle was not content to oppose contrary to contrary and adds grace, that he might print more deeply on the memory that the whole is to be ascribed not to our merit but to the kindness of God. Robertson marks the tenses, an aorist indicative for the throne sin established and an aorist subjunctive for the throne grace might establish, and passes on a judgement that this full rhetorical close has almost the value of a doxology. Barnes observes the triumph celebrated cannot refer to the number of the subjects.
